newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan forces push into eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan forces push into eastern Zaire.

text.p: Rwandan troops attacked the east Zaire city of Goma on Saturday where fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zairean soldiers and militiamen has trapped international aid workers.
I entered Goma behind troops of the Tutsi-led Rwandan army from the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi.
Fighting subsided by late morning in the city, which had been the administrative centre for relief operations for more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees.
There were signs of heavy firing on the buildings and I heard heavy firing south and west of Goma earlier in the day.
Correspondents said a Swedish cameraman was hit by gunfire in Goma on Saturday and taken to hospital in Gisenyi.
The fighting has left more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees inside Zaire in desperate straits, aid workers say.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement from Geneva on Friday night: "Hundreds of thousands of victims -- both Zaireans and refugees -- of the wanton violence raging in Kivu are now left without any form of protection or assistance. It has become impossible to help them...
"The number of civilian casualties is already high and there is a growing fear that the current violence may escalate into a massacre."
Peter Kessler, of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said in Nairobi on Saturday that more than 11,000 Zairean refugees had now fled across the border to southwest Uganda.
He said there had been no reported casualties among the 107 international aid workers in Goma, who are sheltering in basements in the city.
The U.N. Security Council on Friday demanded a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and called on the international community to come up with an urgent response to the crisis.
The United States threw its weight behind a regional conference due to be held in Nairobi next Tuesday which is expected to discuss the conflict.
Rwandan troops first thrust into Goma on Friday by lake and land after mortar and machinegun exchanges with Zairean troops, diplomats said.
On Friday Zairean and Rwandan troops traded fire across the border between the Rwandan town of Gisenyi, at the north end of Lake Kivu, and Goma, the main base for Zaire's army and allied Hutu forces.

The shooting complicated plans by the United Nations to pull out staff from Goma, the centre for largely paralysed efforts to feed and help 1.1 million Rwandan refugees, 200,000 Burundians and tens of thousands of Zaireans uprooted by the fighting.
Zaire's ragged army and allied Rwandan Hutu fighters were facing a humiliating defeat by well-armed rebels in the eastern provinces of North and South Kivu facing Rwanda and Burundi.
All sides ignored international calls for a ceasefire.

Reuters photographer Corinne Dufka reported on Friday that Bukavu, capital of South Kivu, fell to the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels on October 30. She said the rebels controlled the city and it was quiet.
But Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said on Friday the army had retaken Goma and Uvira to the south, which a Reuters correspondent visited on Thursday and reported well in rebel hands.
Bukavu, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Goma, was the scene of some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Zaire and the Roman Catholic archbishop Christophe Munzihirwa was killed on Tuesday.

In the past week, Zairean and Rwandan troops have fired at one another across the border at the only two significant Rwandan towns, Gisenyi and Cyangugu, and Rwanda admitted sending troops into Zaire on a military sortie earlier this week.

The conflict in eastern Zaire pits ethnic Tutsis against both the Zairean government and Hutu refugees, some of whom were responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of up to one million Tutsis and other victims.
UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata has appealed repeatedly for the refugees to go home.
But Tutsi attacks on the camps have pushed the refugees deeper into Zaire and only about 1,000 Rwandans are reported by the U.N. to have crossed into Rwanda.
Many of the refugees have been on the run from fighting for at least a week amid fears they fall to hunger and epidemics.
In their fight with Kinshasa, the Tutsis accuse the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, living since August as an invalid in Switzerland, of persecuting them for years.

The Tutsis trace their roots in Zaire back two centuries. They have been refused Zairean citizenship since 1981 and on Friday Zairean state radio reported that parliament voted to purge Tutsis from the army, state companies and public administration. The move must be approved by the government.
A mob of several hundred demonstrators attacked Tutsi-owned property in Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Friday and looted dozens of cars, a Reuters Television cameraman said.
